analogy.p: Think of an ecosystem as a town. The people (the community) are the living part: they depend on each other as bakers, farmers, teachers and builders (interdependence). The weather, water supply, roads and electricity are the abiotic factors that decide whether the town can function. If the only baker leaves, the cafe, the school canteen and the farmers who sell flour are all affected, just as removing one species disturbs the whole community. If a heatwave cuts the water supply, everyone suffers. People compete for jobs, homes and customers like organisms compete for resources. Where it breaks down: a town is planned and run by people, while an ecosystem has no manager and balances itself through feedback such as predator-prey cycles.

bullets: Define **ecosystem** and describe what the word **community** means.
State what organisms need from their surroundings and from each other to **survive and reproduce**.
State what **plants** compete for (light, space, water, mineral ions from the soil) and what **animals** compete for (food, mates, territory).
Explain **interdependence**: each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and so on, so removing one species can affect the whole community.
Describe a **stable community**: all species and environmental factors are in balance so population sizes stay fairly constant.

Name the seven **abiotic factors**: light intensity, temperature, moisture levels, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity and direction, carbon dioxide levels (for plants), oxygen levels (for aquatic animals).
Name the four **biotic factors**: food availability, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and one species outcompeting another so that numbers are no longer sufficient to breed.
Interpret graphs of **predator-prey cycles** and population data given in unfamiliar contexts.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to understand that every living thing exists inside an **ecosystem**, which is the **interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment**. You must know that organisms need a supply of materials from their surroundings and from other living organisms, that they compete for those materials, and that species depend on one another (**interdependence**). You must also be able to list the **abiotic factors** and the **biotic factors** that affect a community, explain how a change in one of them alters populations, and describe a **stable community**. This is a high-yield topic because it appears on Paper 2 as short recall marks, as graph interpretation and as 4 to 6 mark explanations.

bullets: **Habitat** = where an organism lives (a physical place).
**Population** = all the individuals of **one species** in a habitat.
**Community** = all the populations of **all the different species** in a habitat, interacting with each other.
**Ecosystem** = the **interaction** of a community of living organisms (**biotic**) with the **non-living (abiotic)** parts of their environment.
**Biotic** means living (or caused by living things); **abiotic** means non-living (physical or chemical).
Size does not matter: a puddle, a rotting log, a pond, a woodland and the whole Amazon rainforest are all ecosystems.
Common error: saying a community is 'the animals'. It includes **all** living things, including plants, fungi and microorganisms.
core.h: Key vocabulary: habitat, population, community, ecosystem
core.p: Ecology questions use four nested words and examiners award marks for using them precisely. A **habitat** is the place where an organism lives, for example a pond, a woodland floor or a rocky shore. A **population** is all the organisms of **one species** living in a habitat at the same time, such as all the frogs in the pond. A **community** is all the populations of **different species** living together in a habitat, so the frogs, fish, pondweed, insects and bacteria together form the pond community. An **ecosystem** is bigger again because it includes the community **and** the non-living environment (water, temperature, light, pH) and the way they interact.

bullets: **Plants** need **light** (for photosynthesis), **carbon dioxide** (photosynthesis), **water** (photosynthesis, support, transport) and **mineral ions** from the soil such as nitrate (to make proteins) and magnesium (to make chlorophyll).
**Animals** need **food** (for energy and materials for growth), **water**, **oxygen** (for aerobic respiration), **shelter** and a **mate** to reproduce.
Animals get food by eating **other living organisms** (plants or animals), so the living parts of the community supply their energy and materials.
Plants get **pollinated** and have seeds **dispersed** by animals, so plants also depend on living organisms.
Many organisms need **space or territory** to feed, shelter and breed.
Materials are **recycled**: decomposers break down dead organisms and return mineral ions to the soil, which plants then take in again (carbon and water cycles, covered later).
Because supplies are **limited**, organisms in a community compete.
core.h: What organisms need from their surroundings and from each other
core.p: To **survive and reproduce**, organisms need a supply of materials. Some come from the **abiotic environment** (the surroundings) and some come from **other living organisms** in the community. If a needed material is in short supply, populations are limited, which is why competition happens. Examiners like you to link a specific material to its use, so always say what it is needed for.

bullets: **Light**: leaves need light for photosynthesis. Taller or faster-growing plants shade smaller ones, which then photosynthesise less, grow slower and may die.
**Space**: seeds or seedlings that land close together have less room for roots and leaves. Overcrowded plants are smaller and produce fewer seeds.
**Water**: roots absorb water from the soil. Neighbouring plants with overlapping roots share a limited supply.

**Mineral ions** (for example nitrate and magnesium): taken in through roots by active transport. If nitrate is short, protein synthesis and growth slow; if magnesium is short, leaves lose chlorophyll and turn yellow.
The resources plants compete for are used in **photosynthesis and growth**, so the competition outcome is visible as differences in height, leaf area or biomass.
Example: bluebells flower early in spring in woodland, before the trees grow leaves, so they get light before the canopy shades the floor.
Example: weeds in a crop compete with the crop for light, water and mineral ions and reduce the yield, which is why farmers use herbicides or weed by hand.
core.p: **Competition** is the struggle between organisms for the same limited resource. In a community **plants often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil**. Plants cannot move, so a plant that is shaded by a neighbour or that has roots in a poor patch cannot relocate. The winners grow taller and faster, leave more offspring and pass on their genes, which is part of why competition drives natural selection.

bullets: **Food**: lions and hyenas on the African savanna compete for the same prey; red and grey squirrels compete for the same nuts and seeds.
**Mates**: males of many species fight or display (stags, birds of paradise) to be chosen by females, so the best-adapted males reproduce most.
**Territory**: robins and many other birds defend an area with song and displays; the territory holds food and nest sites.
Competition can be between members of the **same species** (intraspecific, not required wording) or between **different species** (interspecific, not required wording).

If two species need the same limited resource, one may be **outcompeted**. If its numbers fall too low for individuals to find mates, the population may not be able to breed and may die out locally (this is one of the AQA biotic factors).
Example: the introduced grey squirrel has outcompeted the native red squirrel in much of England for food and space, and also spreads a virus that harms red squirrels.
Competition keeps populations roughly in balance with the resources available, because a population cannot keep growing once resources run short.
core.p: **Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.** Food provides the energy and materials animals need to live and grow, mates are needed for sexual reproduction, and a territory is an area defended by an animal that contains the food, shelter and nesting sites it needs. The animals that win more of these resources survive longer and leave more offspring.

bullets: **Food**: herbivores depend on plants; carnivores depend on herbivores; decomposers depend on dead material.
**Shelter**: birds nest in trees, and small animals shelter in leaf litter and burrows, so losing the trees removes homes.
**Pollination**: many plants rely on insects such as bees to transfer pollen, so fewer bees means fewer seeds and fruits.
**Seed dispersal**: animals eat fruit and excrete seeds elsewhere, or carry seeds stuck to fur, so plants depend on animals to spread.
Removing a **producer** affects all the consumers above it. Removing a top predator can let its prey increase and overgraze producers.
Removing a species may allow another competitor to increase, because competition for the same resource falls.
Example: sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze kelp. If otters are removed the urchins increase, the kelp forest is eaten and fish that shelter in the kelp decline.
Stating that species 'depend on each other' earns 1 mark, but explaining **which** dependence and **what** happens next is what earns the rest.
core.p: **Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and so on.** This web of dependence is called **interdependence**. Because of it, **if one species is removed it can affect the whole community**. The effect travels along food chains and through other relationships such as pollination, so a change that seems small can have large knock-on effects. Always describe the chain of cause and effect step by step to earn full marks.

bullets: In a stable community the **processes** such as photosynthesis, feeding, death and decay are in balance, so materials are recycled continually.
Population sizes stay **fairly constant** because birth and death rates roughly match.
Stability is helped by **high biodiversity**: if one species declines, others can take over its role, so the community is more resilient.
Predator-prey relationships help stability: if prey numbers rise, predators increase and push prey back down (a form of **negative feedback**).
A stable community can be **disrupted** by a change in an abiotic factor (drought, pollution) or a biotic factor (a new predator, a new pathogen, an invasive species).
Human activity such as deforestation, pollution, over-hunting and introducing non-native species can make a community unstable.
Exam phrasing: 'all the species and environmental factors are in balance so population sizes remain fairly constant'. Use this almost word for word.
core.p: A **stable community** is one where **all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant** over time. Mineral ions, water and carbon are recycled and the number of each species goes up and down only slightly around an average. Stable does not mean nothing changes; populations still fluctuate, but they do not crash or explode. Examples are a mature oak woodland or a coral reef.

bullets: **Light intensity** (mainly affects plants and algae).
**Temperature** (affects all organisms).
**Moisture levels** (water availability on land).
**Soil pH and mineral content** (affects plants and soil organisms).
**Wind intensity and direction** (affects plants, flying animals and exposed habitats).
**Carbon dioxide levels** (for **plants**).
**Oxygen levels** (for **aquatic animals**).
A useful memory device: **L**ight, **T**emperature, **M**oisture, **S**oil (pH and minerals), **W**ind, **C**O2, **O**2 = 'Lots of Trees Make Soil Wetter, Cooler, Often'.
core.p: **Abiotic factors** are the non-living factors of the environment. AQA lists seven that affect a community. Memorise them as a set because a typical 'state' question asks for three or more. Plants and animals are affected differently, so note which factors apply to which group.

bullets: **Light intensity**: low light means less photosynthesis, so less glucose for growth and respiration. Plants in deep shade or deep water are smaller and fewer, and animals that eat them decline.

**Temperature**: affects the rate of **enzyme-controlled reactions**. Too low and reactions are slow so growth and activity are slow; too high and enzymes **denature**. Cold-blooded animals depend on external temperature to be active.
**Moisture levels**: plants need water for photosynthesis, support and transport, and seeds need water to germinate. In dry conditions plants wilt and fewer survive, so herbivores decline.
**Soil pH**: affects enzyme activity in roots and availability of mineral ions; many plants grow best in a narrow pH range, so acidic or alkaline soil limits which species can grow.
**Mineral content**: nitrate is needed for amino acids and proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll. Low nitrate gives stunted growth, low magnesium gives yellow leaves.

**Wind**: increases the rate of **transpiration**, so plants lose water faster; strong wind can damage plants or blow animals off course and increases cooling and heat loss. Wind direction affects seed and pollen dispersal.
**Carbon dioxide levels** are needed for photosynthesis, so low CO2 can limit plant growth.

**Oxygen levels** in water are needed for aerobic respiration in fish and invertebrates. Warm, polluted or stagnant water holds less dissolved oxygen, so sensitive species such as mayfly larvae disappear.
core.h: How each abiotic factor changes populations (the WHY)
core.p: A change in an abiotic factor changes how well organisms can carry out life processes, and that changes how many can survive. Always link the factor to a **process** (photosynthesis, respiration, enzyme action, water balance) and then to **growth, survival or numbers**. Mark schemes reward the chain: factor, process, effect on organism, effect on population.

bullets: **Light intensity**: light meter (or light sensor).
**Temperature**: thermometer or temperature probe.
**Moisture**: soil moisture meter, or mass of a soil sample before and after drying.
**Soil pH**: pH probe, or soil testing kit with indicator solution.
**Wind**: anemometer for speed, wind vane for direction.
**CO2 and oxygen**: gas sensors or data loggers (dissolved oxygen probe in water).
Take **several readings** at each sampling point and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of random error and anomalies.
A **correlation** (as light falls the number of plants falls) shows a link but does not on its own prove that one factor **causes** the other, because other factors may also change.
core.h: Measuring abiotic factors and analysing data
core.p: You may be given a data table or asked how to measure an abiotic factor in a field investigation. Use appropriate equipment, take **repeated readings** at each site so that you can find a **mean**, and keep other variables the same where possible. Results can then be linked to the distribution of organisms, for example the number of a plant species at different distances from a hedge. This links to the **quadrats and transects required practical**.

bullets: **Availability of food**: if food supply falls (for example a poor crop of berries or a drought reduces plants) then consumers starve or fail to breed, so their numbers fall; more food means more survive and reproduce.
**New predators arriving**: a new predator increases the death rate of its prey, so the prey population falls. Prey with no defences against an introduced predator can be wiped out.

**New pathogens**: a new disease-causing microorganism can spread quickly through a population with no resistance or immunity, raising the death rate and reducing numbers. Example: ash dieback fungus in ash trees.

**One species outcompeting another** so that the numbers of the losing species are no longer sufficient to breed: individuals cannot find mates or enough offspring survive, so the population dies out locally.
A **predator** population rises when prey is plentiful, then falls when prey is scarce.
Biotic factors are often **density dependent** (they have more effect when a population is crowded), whereas many abiotic factors act regardless of density (extension idea, not required).
Biotic and abiotic factors interact: a drought (abiotic) reduces plants, which reduces food (biotic) for herbivores.
core.p: **Biotic factors** are the living factors that affect a community. AQA gives four. Each one changes population size by altering birth rates or death rates. When writing an explanation, name the factor and then trace the effect on each population in turn.

bullets: Step 1: **prey increase** when there is plenty of food and few predators.
Step 2: with more prey available, **predators have more food** so more survive and breed, and the predator population rises (a little later).
Step 3: more predators eat more prey, so the **prey population falls**.
Step 4: with less food, **predator numbers fall** (starvation, fewer offspring), usually after a delay.
Step 5: fewer predators mean fewer prey are eaten, so the **prey recover** and the cycle repeats.
The **prey peak comes before the predator peak**, and the predator peak is lower because it takes many prey to support each predator (see pyramids of numbers and biomass).
In answers, always say **which line** changes first and why, and use the words 'because' and 'so'.
Cycles are idealised; in real data other factors (disease, weather, other food sources) cause irregularity.
core.p: In many communities the numbers of a predator and its prey rise and fall in regular **cycles**. The graph shows two lines on the same axes, with time on the x axis and population size on the y axis. The key pattern is that the **predator curve follows the prey curve with a delay**, and the predator peak is **lower** than the prey peak. This lag is caused by the time it takes for predators to eat, breed and for their young to grow up, and for prey to recover.

bullets: **Abiotic**: temperature, light, rainfall, wind, soil pH, mineral content, salinity, dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide level.
**Biotic**: predators, prey and food availability, competition, pathogens and parasites, mates, pollinators.
Dead leaves or soil minerals are abiotic components, but the **decomposers** that break them down are biotic.
A fire or flood is an abiotic event, but it changes biotic factors afterwards by removing food and shelter.
Humans are part of the community and many 'human impacts' are biotic effects (hunting, introducing species) or change abiotic factors (pollution, climate change).
A single event can have both: pesticide (abiotic chemical) kills insects (biotic loss of food and pollinators).
If asked for **one abiotic and one biotic** factor, give one clearly from each list and say how it affects numbers.
core.h: Abiotic versus biotic: how to classify
core.p: Examiners often give you a list and ask which are abiotic and which are biotic, or ask for one of each. Remember that biotic factors involve **other living organisms** (including their effects such as competition and disease) while abiotic factors are the **physical and chemical** conditions. Some cases catch students out, so learn the borderline examples.

bullets: **Photosynthesis** (4.4.1): light, carbon dioxide, water and temperature are limiting factors; mineral ions are needed for protein and chlorophyll.
**Enzymes**: temperature and pH change enzyme activity, so abiotic factors act on metabolism.
**Adaptations** (next spec point): organisms have features that help them survive particular abiotic and biotic conditions.
**Natural selection and evolution**: competition and predation are selection pressures; better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce.
**Food chains, trophic levels and biomass transfers** show who depends on whom.
**Biodiversity and human impacts**: loss of species disrupts interdependence and reduces stability.
**Carbon and water cycles**: link living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
**Disease** (communicable): new pathogens are a biotic factor.
**Quadrats and transects required practical**: measure how abiotic factors change with distribution of organisms.
core.p: This spec point is the foundation for the rest of Ecology and connects strongly with several other topics. Good answers on Paper 2 draw on these links, especially in the longer 6 mark questions, so know where the ideas reappear.

exam: **State / Name / Give (1 mark each)**: give the exact spec words, such as 'light intensity', 'temperature', 'predators', 'new pathogens'. Do not add extra wrong detail.
**Define ecosystem (usually 1 to 2 marks)**: 'the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment'. Both 'living community' and 'non-living' are needed.
**Name an abiotic and a biotic factor**: choose one clearly from each list; do not say 'weather' (too vague) but 'temperature' or 'rainfall'.
**Explain (2 to 3 marks)**: use a chain: change in factor, effect on process or organism, effect on population ('because', 'so', 'therefore').
**Predator-prey graph (3 to 4 marks)**: say prey rises first, predator rises later, predator peak lower, then describe the repeating cycle and give the reason for the delay (time to feed and breed).
**Reading values**: use a ruler, read both axes with units, and quote data from the graph in any description (for example 'prey fell from 1200 to 400 in 2 years').
**Percentage change**: (new - old) / old x 100. Show the working; give a negative sign or the word 'decrease'.
**6 mark extended answer**: plan with headings (abiotic, biotic, links), include at least two factors with a full chain each, and finish with a conclusion on stability.
**Evaluate data**: mention sample size, repeats, correlation does not prove causation, and other factors that were not controlled.

mistakes.r: A community is all the populations of different species (plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms) living together in a habitat.
mistakes.w: A community is just all the animals in an area.

mistakes.r: Abiotic means non-living (physical or chemical), such as temperature or soil pH. Dead organisms are the remains of living things, and the decomposers that break them down are biotic.
mistakes.w: Abiotic factors are things that are dead.

mistakes.r: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. They compete for light, space, water and mineral ions from the soil.
Animals compete for food, mates and territory (and water and shelter).
mistakes.w: Animals compete for light and minerals.

mistakes.r: More predators mean more prey are eaten, so prey numbers fall. Predator numbers follow prey numbers with a delay.
mistakes.w: Predator numbers go up, so prey go up too.

mistakes.r: Population sizes stay fairly constant because the species and environmental factors are in balance; they may still fluctuate slightly.
mistakes.w: In a stable community nothing changes.

mistakes.r: Because of interdependence the whole community can be affected: its prey, its competitors, the plants it pollinated and so on.
mistakes.w: If a species is removed, only its predator is affected.

mistakes.r: Say how: high temperature denatures enzymes so reactions stop; low temperature slows enzyme-controlled reactions so growth and activity fall.
The predator peak comes after the prey peak and is lower; describe the delay and give the reason.
mistakes.w: The graph shows both lines peak at the same time.

summary: AQA 4.7.1 (communities, abiotic and biotic factors): you must define an ecosystem as the interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of the environment, explain competition and interdependence, describe a stable community, and name the seven abiotic and four biotic factors and explain how each changes populations. It matters because it underpins all of Ecology and appears on Paper 2 in recall, graph and 6 mark questions.

terms.d: The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
The place where an organism lives.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat.
All the populations of different species living together in a habitat and interacting with each other.
A living factor that affects a community, such as food availability, predators, pathogens and competition.
A non-living factor that affects a community, such as light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content, wind, carbon dioxide and oxygen levels.
The struggle between organisms for the same limited resource, such as light, space, water, mineral ions, food, mates or territory.
Each species in a community depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and so on, so removing one species can affect the whole community.
A community where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
An animal that hunts and kills other animals (its prey) for food.
An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
An organism, usually a green plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis and starts a food chain.
An area defended by an animal that contains the resources (food, shelter, nest sites) it needs.
When one species is better than another at getting a limited resource, so the other species' numbers fall.
Dissolved nutrients absorbed by plant roots from the soil, for example nitrate and magnesium.

worked.ans: Both populations rise and fall in a repeating cycle. Rabbit numbers peak first and the fox peak comes later and is lower. When rabbit numbers are high there is more food, so more foxes survive and reproduce and fox numbers rise. More foxes eat more rabbits so rabbit numbers fall. With less food, fox numbers then fall, fewer rabbits are eaten and rabbit numbers recover, so the cycle repeats.
worked.q: The graph shows the number of rabbits (prey) and foxes (predators) over 12 years. Describe and explain the pattern shown by the two populations. (4 marks)
steps: Describe: both populations rise and fall in repeating cycles (1).
The rabbit peak comes before the fox peak, and the fox peak is lower (1).
Explain the rise: when rabbits increase there is more food for foxes, so foxes survive and breed and increase later (1).
Explain the fall: more foxes eat more rabbits so rabbits fall; then foxes starve or breed less and fall, so rabbits recover (1).

worked.ans: (a) 25% decrease (-25%). (b) A biotic factor (new pathogen). With fewer rabbits there is less food for foxes, so fox numbers fall.
worked.q: Rabbit numbers in a field fell from 1200 to 900 after a new disease arrived. (a) Calculate the percentage change. (b) Name the type of factor that caused the fall and explain the effect on the foxes that eat the rabbits. (4 marks)
steps: Percentage change = -300 / 1200 x 100 = -25%. This is a 25% decrease.
(b) A new pathogen is a biotic factor.
Fewer rabbits means less food for foxes, so fox numbers will fall (they starve or breed less); this shows interdependence.

worked.ans: Biotic: a new predator increases the death rate; less insect food reduces survival and breeding. Abiotic: very low temperature or strong wind increases heat loss and reduces survival of adults and chicks. Together these reduce the population.
worked.q: A farmer notices that the population of a bird species in a hedgerow has fallen. Suggest two biotic and one abiotic reason, explaining each. (6 marks)
steps: Biotic 1: a new predator arrives (for example a cat), so more birds are killed and the death rate rises (2).
Biotic 2: food availability falls (for example insects fall because pesticide was used), so birds starve or fail to rear chicks (2).
Abiotic: a cold or windy spell reduces the temperature, so birds lose more heat and use more energy; chicks may die (2).
